title: sandhi plainly
hook: a y that sneaks in when words are said fast, welcome as well come, and a Gita line that opens once an i is put back
tomorrow: Jagannath means lord of the world. so where's the world?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi plainly at its most serious: two a's melting into one, and a line two schools split two ways. Today, a join you can feel your own mouth make.

Say see it, fast, a few times. Somewhere in there a little y sneaks in: see-yit. Nobody taught the mouth that. It just slid from one vowel to the next. Sanskrit noticed the slide, and wrote it down. Svagatam, welcome, comes apart into two words: su, well, and agatam, come. Well come. But the u at the end of su didn't vanish. It became a v.
screen: `SEE IT, SAID FAST.` → `A Y SNEAKS IN.` → `SU + AGATAM = SVAGATAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the join. When i or u meets a different vowel, it turns into the consonant closest to it. I becomes y. U becomes v. Panini says it in three words: iko yan aci. That last word, aci, means before a vowel, the shorthand from Shiva's drum, ac for every vowel. So su plus agatam gives svagatam. Iti, thus, plus adi, the rest, gives ityadi: and so on. Now a line from the Bhagavad Gita, chapter two. Krishna tells Arjuna that his right is to action alone, never to its fruit. In Sanskrit, the line opens karmany eva. A dictionary won't list karmany. Undo the join. Karmani, in action, ends in i. Eva, alone, begins with e. The i became a y. Karmani eva: in action alone. A few words later comes the fruit itself, a form of phala, the word with the breathy p. One small undoing, and a line that might only have been heard in translation can be read word by word. And the mouth already knew the rule. It made the same slide every time see it was said fast.
screen: `I BECOMES Y. U BECOMES V.` · `IKO YAN ACI.` · `KARMANY EVA, UNDONE.` · `THE MOUTH ALREADY KNEW.` · then, large: `KARMANI + EVA.`

segments.voice: Without making a sound, let the mouth glide slowly from i into a, and feel the tongue pass through a y on its own; then from u into a, and feel the lips pass through a v. Let each glide get slower than the last, until the mouth rests and only the breath is moving.
Sandhi plainly: today, i turning into y and u turning into v, to make room for the vowel that follows.
For the road: sandhi plainly, where undoing one join can open a whole line. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sanskrit students practice undoing joins on lines they already know, and karmany evadhikaras te, from the Gita's second chapter, is a line some teachers use for it.

chat.says: practicing my line fast and my mouth keeps slipping a y between words. am i ruining it?
options: not ruining it: i before a vowel slides into y; Sanskrit writes it down.
yes: in Sanskrit, every word should stay fully separate when spoken.
that's just an accent; Sanskrit vowels never turn into consonants.
chat.meaning: Panini's iko yan aci: i and u turn into y and v before a different vowel. The mouth's slide is the rule.
